item.title: The case for a personal changelog
item.description:
Every repo I own keeps a CHANGELOG.md, and beyond that there is one plain text file with the things that do not belong to a repo: a firewall rule, a DNS entry, a systemd unit that exists for a reason I will not remember.

The format is deliberately boring — date, what changed, why, and how to undo it. Ten seconds per entry, and it has already answered “why is this port open” twice this year.

item.title: Riding OneDrive on Linux (it still hurts)
item.description:
There is no first-party client, so the realistic options are a browser or the abraunegg client. The client wins on the one thing that matters: it can be trusted to run headless as a systemd user service.

First run goes out with --dry-run and a conflict policy I chose on purpose (--resync is the sledgehammer; read what it deletes before running it). Inotify watches on a large tree need fs.inotify.max_user_watches raised, and the sync log is the actual interface — read it or be surprised.

item.title: Testcontainers with rootless Podman
item.description:
I run Podman rootless, which means the Docker socket Testcontainers expects simply is not there. The fix is one environment pair and a socket path that actually exists:

1
2

export DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/user/$(id -u)/podman/podman.sock
export TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true

Ryuk needs a socket it can mount, and the rootless one is not it. Without Ryuk you own cleanup — a nightly podman ps --filter label=... sweep handles leftovers.

Two gotchas survived consolidation. The socket must be running (systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket), and Docker.DotNet caches the endpoint per process — set the variables before the first client is constructed, not inside a fixture.

item.title: Renovate, but for your compose files
item.description:
The mental model that unlocked Renovate for me: it is a match-and-replace engine, and the package ecosystems are just presets. A customManagers regex entry makes any version string in any file a dependency.

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

{
 "customManagers": [{
 "customType": "regex",
 "fileMatch": ["docker-compose\\.ya?ml$"],
 "matchStrings": ["image: (?<depName>\\S+):(?<currentValue>\\S+)"],
 "datasourceTemplate": "docker"
 }]
}

The value is not freshness for its own sake — it is that the bump arrives as a pull request on a quiet morning instead of as a surprise during an incident. Digest pinning plus grouping keeps the noise proportional to the risk.

item.title: Blazor JS interop without the ceremony
item.description:
The interop that bites is the one called too early. During prerender there is no JavaScript, so anything in OnInitializedAsync that touches IJSRuntime either throws or silently no-ops depending on the render mode.

The shape that has held up: import the module once, keep the IJSObjectReference, call it in OnAfterRenderAsync(firstRender: true), and release it in IAsyncDisposable.

1
2
3
4
5
6
7
8

private IJSObjectReference? module;

protected override async Task OnAfterRenderAsync(bool firstRender)
{
 if (!firstRender) return;
 module = await JS.InvokeAsync<IJSObjectReference>("import", "./chart.js");
 await module.InvokeVoidAsync("draw", elementRef);
}

One import per component instance is fine at this scale; the ceremony people add around shared module caching is a different problem.

item.title: systemd timers without the ceremony
item.description:
Cron keeps getting replaced by two files that do what cron does plus logs, dependencies, and catch-up runs. The minimum pair:

1
2
3
4

# backup.timer
[Timer]
OnCalendar=daily
Persistent=true

with a Type=oneshot service beside it. Persistent=true is the one directive cron cannot give you: a missed run catches up after boot instead of silently skipping.

systemctl list-timers is the whole dashboard, and journalctl -u backup.service is the whole log story. RandomizedDelaySec on anything that phones home avoids the thundering herd at midnight.

item.title: Pull requests as reading practice
item.description:
I read pull requests I am not assigned to. Not to comment on every one — the habit is reading, and leaving a question only where a question is genuinely owed.

Fifteen minutes a day buys context that status meetings cannot: where the codebase is actually moving, which abstractions are straining, and who is about to need help.

The failure mode is turning reading into reviewing. Unrequested nitpicks cost the team more than the missed typo ever would; the rule I keep is that the comment must be worth the author’s next ten minutes.

item.title: Flaky tests are a scheduling problem
item.description:
Chasing a flaky test as a mystery wastes days. Chasing it as a scheduling bug is usually one afternoon, because the suspects are three: shared state between tests, dependence on wall-clock time, and dependence on real IO order.

The fixes are correspondingly boring. Fixtures that cannot leak (async setup/teardown per test, no static caches), a fake clock injected rather than DateTime.Now, and a container per suite instead of a shared database with yesterday’s rows.

item.title: Espresso: preinfusion by feel
item.description:
Wetting the puck at low flow for three to five seconds before opening the pump costs nothing and forgives a lot: fewer channeling spurts, and the first drops arrive sweeter instead of sharp.

It is not pressure profiling — it is one gesture, done by hand, at the lever. On my machine that is easing the pump on and counting. The puck saturates more evenly, so I can grind a notch finer and still hit the same time.

item.title: Recovering Lost Changes with JetBrains Rider Local History
item.description: Local History is one of those IDE features you don't think about until you desperately need it. This post covers what it is, how it works, and the scenarios where it saves you: accidental rollbacks, lost uncommitted changes and rebase mistakes.

item.title: Btrfs snapshots before you need them
item.description:
Hourly snapshots cost nothing until data changes, which is the point: the price of the safety net is the data you replaced, not the files you kept.

The detail that trips everyone: a snapshot of the root subvolume does not include the other subvolumes. /home living as its own subvolume means the home snapshots are a separate schedule, or they are silently absent.

Rollback is where I stop improvising. btrfs subvolume set-default <id> / and a reboot beats moving directories around by hand — and doing it once in advance, on purpose, is what makes it boring when it matters.

item.title: Backups that survive you: restic and B2
item.description:
One restic repository per machine, encrypted with a passphrase that lives somewhere other than the machine. Backups run from a systemd timer, and the retention policy is explicit:

1

restic forget --keep-daily 7 --keep-weekly 5 --keep-monthly 12 --prune

Backblaze B2 holds the repo because it is cheap and boring, which is the highest praise storage can get.

The part that makes it a backup rather than a hope: a monthly restore drill that pulls three random files to /tmp and diffs them. An untested backup is a rumor.

item.title: WireGuard at home, the boring way
item.description:
One key pair per peer, one config file per peer, wg-quick up — and then it stays up across reboots via the systemd unit, which is the part people reinvent.

The home side allows exactly one CIDR and one port. The other side routes nothing except that CIDR; split tunnel by default, because my laptop belongs to hotels as much as to me.

MTU 1420 belongs in every config on a consumer router, and the first symptom of getting it wrong is the one that sends people back to logs: SSH works, large pushes hang. That note has saved me an afternoon twice.

item.title: A field guide to NuGet central package management
item.description:
Central package management moves every version into one Directory.Packages.props, and suddenly “which version is this solution on” has one answer instead of forty.

The migration order that worked: add the props file, ManagePackageVersionsCentrally, strip versions from every csproj, restore, then fix the one project that legitimately disagrees with a VersionOverride — and write a comment explaining why, because future-you will delete it otherwise.

Transitive pinning is the sharp edge: it can unify versions that were quietly different, so I run the full test suite after the first central restore, not after tidying the props file.

item.title: Delta: the git pager I should have known about
item.description:
The diff is the most-read output in a developer’s day, and it looked like 1998 until I set two lines:

1
2
3
4

[core]
 pager = delta
[interactive]
 diffFilter = delta --color-only

Side-by-side mode for reviewing my own work before pushing, unified for reading a PR, and line numbers so “the third hunk” becomes a coordinate instead of a description.

It changes nothing about git. It changes how much of the diff I actually read, which changes what I catch before anyone else has to.

item.title: AWS SSO for personal accounts
item.description:
A personal AWS account deserves the same credential hygiene as a company one, and Identity Center makes it cheap: one admin user, one permission set, and aws configure sso writing profiles into ~/.aws/config.

After that, the muscle memory is --profile, and the long-lived access keys that used to live in ~/.aws/credentials are deleted. Nothing hangs off root except the billing alarm.

The cost is a browser login every eight hours. That is the feature.

item.title: Hario Switch: the recipe I keep
item.description:
Twenty grams in, 300 out, water at 93. Bloom with 60 grams for forty seconds with the switch closed, pour to 150 by the minute, then open the switch and pour the rest in circles.

The switch is the part that earned its place: a closed steep at the start makes the first pour forgiving of a wobbly kettle, and the drawdown stays even when the grind drifts a click.

item.title: C# collection expressions in real code
item.description:
int[] a = [1, 2, 3] is tidy, but the syntax earns its keep in expressions, not declarations: spread operators turn “new list from those items plus this one” into one line instead of a loop or a AddRange.

1

var targets = [.. defaults, .. overrides, extra];

Two places I still write it out: public APIs where the concrete type is part of the contract, and anywhere the compiler silently picks Span<T> and the benchmark disagrees with the aesthetics.

item.title: Reading notes: A Philosophy of Software Design
item.description:
The book’s durable idea for me is the deep module: an interface narrow enough to hold in your head over an implementation big enough to be worth hiding. Every time I have split a class “for single responsibility” and ended up with three shallow wrappers, this is the counterweight.

The second: complexity is anything that makes a future change harder, and dependencies are the main supplier. That definition turns design arguments into questions with answers — what would this make harder, for whom, when.

item.title: Creating a Maintainable Resume with Markdown and Pandoc
item.description: Keeping a professional resume updated and adaptable for various applications can be a challenging. This post demonstrates how leveraging Markdown for content and Pandoc for conversion simplifies the process, enabling you to maintain a single, clean source file that effortlessly transforms into polished PDF, DOCX, or HTML outputs.

item.title: Down the Rabbit Hole of creating a Home Lab
item.description: Setting up a home lab is an incredible journey that opens up countless learning opportunities in system administration, networking, security, and modern deployment practices. While it might seem daunting at first, the knowledge gained is invaluable for any tech enthusiast or IT professional. In this post, I'll share a practical overview of how I use my home lab, highlighting the real-world projects I've tackled and the key lessons learned along the way. From self-hosting essential services to experimenting with automation, networking, and security, I'll focus on the hands-on experiences that have shaped my understanding of home server management and modern IT practices.

item.title: Server-side rendered SPAs with ASP.NET and no Javascript
item.description: Single-page applications (SPA) provide better user experience by removing full-page loads, giving smooth transitions between pages and performance improvements depending on the scale of the application, but they come at some costs which may not be worth for some application types. The main cost is the added complexity of a SPA framework like Angular or Vue. In this post, I'll show how to use ASP.NET and HTMX to build single-page applications without using JavaScript and SPA frameworks.

item.title: Integration tests with AWS S3 buckets using Localstack and Testcontainers
item.description: As I explained previously in this article, in integration tests, we should mock unmanaged dependencies (dependencies that are external to our system and not controlled by us, like APIs) but test against real managed dependencies (dependencies that are controlled by our system, like databases, queues, etc). This improves the reliability of the integration tests because the communication with these dependencies are a complex part of the system and can break with a package update, a database update or a change in a queue message format. In this post, I'll show how to use Localstack and Testcontainers to emulate an AWS environment for use in integration tests.

item.title: Lessons learned from building a static code analyzer for C#
item.description: Static code analyzers are tools used to analyze software code without executing it. They can examine the code to find code smells, vulnerabilities, potential errors, and code out of a defined standard, for example. They work by parsing the source code and evaluating its syntax (structure of the code) and semantic (meaning of the code). Roslyn, the C# compiler, provides tools for developing Roslyn Analyzers (Static code analyzers for Roslyn), giving access to the syntax and semantic of the code, that can be executed at development and build time, providing feedback in near real-time to the developers. In this post, I'll show a Roslyn Analyzer I built for using Discriminated Unions in C#, requiring to check the union type before access, and talk about some lessons learned while developing it.

item.title: Building a Who's that Pokémon game for Android with .NET MAUI and Blazor Hybrid
item.description: Blazor was initially developed to build interactive web applications using C#, but can now be used in many platforms when used together with .NET MAUI. In this post, I'll show how to use Blazor Hybrid to develop a Who's that Pokémon game for Android.

item.title: How to run scripts on SQL Server container startup
item.description: Unlike MySQL and PostgreSQL, which execute scripts in the /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/ directory after initialization, the SQL Server container image doesn't provide a built-in mechanism for running scripts at startup. In this post, I'll show how to create a custom container image that waits for SQL Server startup and runs a pre-configured script. In addition, I'll show how to use this custom image to run SQL Server in Testcontainers.

item.title: Why my WireMock mocks aren't working?
item.description: WireMock.Net is a great tool to remove external dependencies when writing integration tests, but because it is highly configurable, it can be hard to find why its mocks aren't working. In this post, I'll explain how to troubleshoot problems in its configuration and show some common problems that happen in my day-to-day work.

item.title: .NET and AWS S3 with LocalStack: How to develop with local S3 buckets
item.description: LocalStack is an open-source framework that allows us to emulate the major AWS services locally, making it easier to develop and test cloud applications without incurring the cost and complexity of deploying to a real cloud environment. In this post, I'll show how to configure it to emulate S3 buckets and how to interact with those buckets from a C# application.

item.title: How to use C# 11 features in .NET 6 or older versions (even .NET Framework 2.0)
item.description: At each release, C# adds features that help us make our codes cleaner, more readable and more maintainable. The problem is that, because some features are dependent of runtime implementations, C# versions are generally tied to .NET runtime versions. For example, C# 11 is enabled only in .NET 7 and above. In this post, I'll show how to use C# 11 in older runtime version (even .NET Framework 2.0).

item.title: How to run disposable databases for your tests. Improve your integration tests accuracy with Testcontainers
item.description: Integration tests are essential to ensure that the different components of our system work together as expected and continue to work after changes. In this post, I'll explain how to spin up disposable database containers to use in integration tests.

item.title: Time-out requests in ASP.NET Core with cancellation tokens
item.description: When ASP.NET Core is running in an AWS Lambda and receiving requests through an AWS API Gateway, the application is not notified of an API Gateway time-out and keeps processing the request, completing it eventually. This will leave metrics and logs of a successful request when the client received a time-out error. In this post, I'll show how to solve this problem with cancellation tokens and time-outs.

item.title: Canceling abandoned requests in ASP.NET Core
item.description: When a client makes an HTTP request, the client can abort the request, leaving the server processing if it's not prepared to handle this scenario; wasting its resources that could be used to process other jobs. In this post, I'll show how to use Cancellation Tokens to cancel running requests that were aborted by clients.

item.title: Keep your diagrams updated with continuous delivery
item.description: Changing software diagrams is hard. The simple act of adding a new box may require us to drag all the existing boxes and reorganize the diagram. This is one of the main reasons to why software diagrams are constantly left deprecated after the first stages of the development process. In this post I'll show how defining diagrams as code can help in designing and updating software diagrams, and how to automate the process of updating the documentation with those diagrams.

item.title: Cleaner representation of software architectures with the C4 Model
item.description: Diagrams are a great way to visually communicate something. However, the majority of software architecture diagrams don't really express what they intend to, lacking description of its elements and with lots of implicit notations only understood by who drew the diagram. Also, they try to express more than one vision (high level, infrastructure, flow order, etc) in only one diagram, making it even harder for non technical people or people outside the project to understand. In this post, I'll present the C4 model and how it can produce software architecture diagrams that are inclusive to non-technical people, easier to understand and, consequently, better to document our software systems.

item.title: Analyzing and enforcing .NET code coverage with coverlet
item.description: Automated software tests are a requirement for ensuring we are delivering a product with quality to our users. It helps in finding bugs and requirements not fulfilled at development time, but also decreases the cost of maintenance by making the future changes to our code safer. Besides, the act of writing testable code alone increases the quality of the code we are writing because testable code has to be decoupled. In this last post of this series, I'll show how to analyze and enforce a minimum code coverage in our applications, and how to use integration tests to increase our testing surface.

item.title: Enforcing .NET code style rules at compile time
item.description: Static code analysis is a great tool for spotting some kinds of error in your code, for example, not disposing of objects that implement IDisposable. Also, it helps to enforce and validate if the code written is following a defined standard, for example, using PascalCase for class names and camelCase for parameter names. In this post I'll show how to use Roslyn Analyzers with C# to enforce some standards of code quality and code style on your code, throwing errors at compile time if any rules are not being respected and not allowing the code to be pushed to protected branches of the repository.

item.title: Defining formatting rules in .NET with EditorConfig
item.description: When working with other people and multiple editors/IDEs, it is common to have different editor settings, losing consistency in formatting styles of the code. For example: Using tabs/spaces and different sizes of indentation, making your code harder to read; Using different encoding between files, causing hard to find bugs at runtime (showing invalid characters) and breaking automated tests. In this post I'll show how to maintain a standard for everyone who works in the code, no matter the editor used, and in a next post I'll show how to enforce these (and other) rules on build and in the continuous integration pipeline.

item.title: Integration tests without API dependencies with ASP.NET Core and WireMock.Net
item.description: Although there are many definitions about the scope of an integration test, Martin Fowler defines Narrow integration tests, where the integration with other systems are tested using mocks, and Broad integration tests, where they communicate using real APIs. In this post, I'll explain how to create mocks for HTTP APIs in narrow integration tests using the WireMock.Net library.

item.title: The Garden
